title: The true yogi
hookLine: a true yogi is one who lives the Guru's teaching in ordinary life

cards: What does a yogi look like? Ask around and the answers come quickly. Someone thin, cross-legged on a mountain, far from phones and rent.
Ash on the skin, maybe. Big earrings. A staff.
Silence. The Siddhs in the Sidh Gosht looked something like that, and they had paid for it: they had left homes and families to live apart.
Across from them sits Nanak, who, tradition says, went home to a family and fields. So a question hangs over the whole conversation: where is yoga found?

teach.b: In the Sidh Gosht, Nanak's answer keeps returning to one figure: the Gurmukh, the person turned toward the Guru. It is the Gurmukh who finds the way of yoga, through the Word.
The old phrase for it is jog jugat, the method of yoga. Nanak doesn't throw the phrase out. He fills it with something else.
A short hymn of his in Raga Suhi sits beside the Sidh Gosht like a summary.

teach.h: NOT THE COAT, NOT THE STAFF.
teach.b: In paraphrase: yoga is not the patched coat, not the staff, not ash rubbed on the body. It isn't earrings or a shaved head or the blowing of a horn.

teach.h: SPOTLESS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SOOT.
teach.b: Then the line that turns it: stay spotless in the middle of the soot. That is how the way of yoga is found. Soot.
That's the picture. Not a clean mountain far away, but the smoky kitchen, the office, the crowded bus, the family argument. The test isn't whether you can stay pure where nothing touches you.

It's whether you can stay clear where everything does. That's why Sikh teaching honors the householder: someone who earns a living, cooks, cares for the young and the old, and keeps the Name through all of it.
The yogis' discipline was real, and Nanak doesn't call them lazy.
He moves the discipline indoors, into the hours most people already live.
A true yogi, in this reading, might be wiping a counter right now, or waiting in a slow checkout line, steady. The coat and the staff aren't the point. The way you do the next ordinary thing is.

how: Sikh teaching honors the householder's life: Sikhs are encouraged to work, raise families and serve others while keeping the Name, rather than leaving home for the forest.

o: a householder who stays clear in daily life
someone who masters postures and the breath
a hermit who leaves home for the mountains

games.q: what's inside the true yogi — tap the pairs.
p: the way, or method, of yoga
the one turned toward the Guru
stay spotless in the middle of it

s: Nanak tells the yogis their discipline is worthless
he keeps their phrase, the way of yoga, and fills it with the Word lived in ordinary life.
the Suhi hymn says yoga is found by staying spotless amid the soot
not in the coat, the staff or the ashes.
Sikh teaching asks seekers to leave home to find God
it honors the householder who keeps the Name while working and raising a family.

games.q: the Siddhs have left their homes for the mountain. where is yoga truly found, in Nanak's answers?
o: in the coat, the staff and the ashes.
far from people, on the mountain.
in ordinary life, spotless in the middle of the soot.
games.why: the Gurmukh finds the way through the Word, in ordinary life. the soot doesn't disqualify anyone; it's where the practice happens.

practice: Pick one ordinary thing close by, a cup to wash, a shirt to fold, a plant to water, and give it your whole attention, its weight, its temperature, its sound, the way the yogis gave theirs to the breath.
When your mind runs ahead to the next job, bring it back to this one. If you pray, keep the Name in mind while your hands work; if you don't, the full attention is enough.

wordCard.voice: The true yogi. In Nanak's answer, the Gurmukh, who keeps the Word in ordinary life and stays spotless in the middle of the soot. Today's word.

orig.note: jog: yoga, as the Guru Granth Sahib writes it; jog jugat is the way of yoga.

carryVoice: Your line: yoga in daily life. The soot is where the way is found. That's the mountain for today.
